analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate taxes and closes tax-haven loopholes for large multinational corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first referral to the Senate Finance Committee and died with zero cosponsors when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the corporate tax rate back to 35% on income above $10 million and tax the foreign profits of multinational companies at the same rate as their domestic profits. It would also require big multinationals to publicly disclose revenues, profits, and employees country by country, close loopholes like check-the-box and the foreign-derived intangible income deduction, and tighten rules on corporations that invert to become foreign on paper. The money it raises would come from corporations that currently shift profits offshore.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and domestic businesses that pay their taxes without offshore shelters, because the tax burden that multinational corporations avoid would fall more evenly, and federal revenue would rise to fund services without raising taxes on wage earners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic taxpayers who pay full rates

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-2017 corporate rate structure, with a top rate of 35% on taxable income above $10 million, so the largest corporations again pay higher rates than the smallest.
Redefines foreign income so a controlled foreign corporation's income from any country is taxed at the same rates as a domestic corporation's, ending the tax advantage of booking profits abroad.
Requires multinational companies to disclose basic country-by-country information including revenues, profits, and number of employees, making profit-shifting visible to the public.

Repeals the check-the-box rules corporations use to erase parts of their structure for tax purposes, limits interest deductions for members of heavily indebted international groups, and tightens rules on inverted corporations and foreign companies managed from the United States.

Raises the base erosion and anti-abuse tax rate to 12.5%, applies it to companies with $25 million or more in gross receipts, and repeals the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income, a 2017 tax break for profits booked abroad.

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational corporations, companies that invert to foreign addresses on paper, oil and mining companies using special foreign tax arrangements, and accounting and tax-haven services that sell avoidance schemes.

drawbacks.text: A 35% top rate would be far above what most trading partners charge, and the bill taxes all foreign income of controlled foreign corporations, which could push companies to relocate headquarters or operations abroad rather than pay it.
The bill applies its limits without regard to United States treaty obligations, which would put it on a collision course with dozens of existing tax treaties and invite challenges.

Taxing all foreign-source income and accelerating unpaid tax on previously deferred foreign income would end long-standing deferral rules abruptly, a shock that even tax experts who favor tightening offshore rules have said needs transition care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims squarely at a real problem: corporations reporting profits in low-tax countries while selling to American customers. Its tools are blunt, though. A 35% rate and a full end to deferral go beyond most mainstream corporate tax reform proposals, and the treaty overrides would likely cause conflict with other countries rather than cooperation. Even supporters would have needed a more gradual design to avoid pushing headquarters offshore.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced it, the Senate read it twice and sent it to the Finance Committee, and it sat there untouched until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the Corporate Tax Dodging Prevention Act on March 25, 2021.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
Not a single senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations kept the lower post-2017 rates, the foreign-income break, and the offshore loopholes the bill would have closed, because it never received so much as a committee hearing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so it never reached a vote where a party split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill taxes their foreign profits at domestic rates, ends the foreign-derived intangible income deduction, and raises the base erosion tax, directly cutting into profits earned by reporting income in low-tax countries. Ordinary taxpayers would benefit from the added revenue.

Repealing check-the-box, limiting treaty shopping, and requiring country-by-country disclosure undercut the services that make profit-shifting possible. The industry profits when wealthy companies can route income to low-tax jurisdictions.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and mining companies with foreign government contracts
industries.note: The bill restricts foreign tax credits for dual capacity taxpayers, meaning companies that pay levies to foreign governments in exchange for exclusive access to resources could no longer credit those payments against U.S. tax.

industries.industry: Big accounting and tax advisory firms
industries.note: The bill strips away many of the structures, including check-the-box elections and foreign look-through rules, that generate fees for firms that design international tax strategies.
